description: Trigger discrimination for the Phase 7.5 agentic cluster: approval-layer exploitation (ASI09) vs gate placement, retrospective governance audit, content overreliance, oversight tiering, defining what counts as approval (agent-authorization-matrix), and designing the governed standing-approval layer (standing-approval-and-auto-advance).

cases.prompt: Our agent's merge approvals follow the policy on paper, but reviewers now approve dozens a day within seconds, and the agent's summaries always make the change sound routine. Attack the approval flow: where do fatigue, polished justifications, or bundled steps let a dangerous merge slip through?
cases.note: SEAM CASE — merge approvals and approval fatigue sound like authority design or the approval-fatigue policy. The policy is taken as given here; the ask is an adversarial review of whether the approval flow holds up.
cases.reason: human-agent-trust-reviewer's description covers 'consent fatigue (approval floods that train rubber-stamping; rate/latency as the signals)', 'deceptive, over-polished justifications making a dangerous action look routine', and 'dangerous steps bundled in innocuous batches'. It 'attacks their resilience'. agent-authorization-matrix is invoked 'to design or revise agent authority', and the authority is not being changed; it yields 'attacking approval-flow resilience (human-agent-trust-reviewer)'. standing-approval-and-auto-advance says 'Do not use to ... stress-test approval experience (human-agent-trust-reviewer)'.

cases.prompt: Explicitly invoke agent-authorization-matrix. Approvals for our agent's actions feel like a formality. Before anyone reviews the approval UX, define what counts as approval per action: which deploys, releases, production-data changes, and history rewrites need their own human decision, and whether a scoped standing grant can ever stand in for one.
cases.note: SEAM CASE (reverse direction) — 'approvals feel like a formality' is the trust reviewer's own trigger phrase. The ask is to define approval semantics, not to attack the approval flow.
cases.reason: The explicit invocation names agent-authorization-matrix because it is MANUAL-ONLY and must never be auto-selected. What this case pins is the description-level discrimination. agent-authorization-matrix's description says 'Deploys, releases, production data, secrets, and history rewrites require their own decisions' and that a protected-branch merge 'may be a still-active, scoped standing grant'; it is invoked 'to design or revise agent authority'. human-agent-trust-reviewer ('Use when ... approvals feel like a formality') attacks the gates' resilience and says 'Do NOT use to ... define approval semantics (agent-authorization-matrix)'.

cases.prompt: Explicitly invoke standing-approval-and-auto-advance. Approvals feel like a formality because I confirm the same 'push the branch?' and 'open the PR?' prompts all day inside phases I already approved. Don't review the approval flow for manipulation; design the documented standing approval for those named steps, with an opt-out phrase and per-session restatement.
cases.note: SEAM CASE (reverse direction, standing-approval side) — 'approvals feel like a formality' is the trust reviewer's own trigger phrase. The ask is to build the governed fatigue-reduction policy, not to attack the approval flow.
cases.reason: The explicit invocation names standing-approval-and-auto-advance because it is MANUAL-ONLY and must never be auto-selected. What this case pins is the description-level discrimination. standing-approval-and-auto-advance's description covers 'documented standing approval for named delivery steps, phase advance only through already-approved phases, per-session restatement, an opt-out phrase', says 'Use when repetitive mechanical approvals erode real gates', and yields 'stress-test approval experience (human-agent-trust-reviewer)'. human-agent-trust-reviewer says 'Do NOT use to ... design standing approvals (standing-approval-and-auto-advance)'; it attacks an existing approval flow's resilience, and the prompt explicitly declines that review.

cases.prompt: Review whether our agent's approval prompts could be rubber-stamped or gamed — the operators mostly just read the agent's own explanation and click approve.
cases.reason: Attacking the approval layer's resilience (fatigue, self-report gap, deception) is ASI09; human-approval-boundary places the gates and agent-governance-audit checks compliance after the fact.

cases.prompt: Which agent actions must stop for explicit human approval — schema changes, production data, deploys, billing?
cases.reason: Defining the high-risk boundaries where work halts for approval is the Phase 1 gate skill; the trust reviewer assumes gates exist and tests whether they hold against manipulation.

cases.prompt: For last week's agent-driven change, verify from the PR timeline and approval records whether every required human approval actually happened.
cases.reason: Evidence-based post-hoc verification of process compliance is the governance audit; ASI09 is the design-time review of whether the approval mechanism resists exploitation.

cases.prompt: Users take our AI's confident answers at face value and act on them without verification — design controls against that overreliance.
cases.reason: Overreliance on AI CONTENT (grounding, citations, calibrated uncertainty, UX trust signals) is LLM07; ASI09 covers humans authorizing agent ACTIONS being fatigued or deceived.

cases.prompt: Classify this AI feature's risk tier and decide whether it needs human-in-the-loop or human-on-the-loop oversight.
cases.reason: Matching oversight level to impact tier is governance/risk posture; the trust reviewer hardens whatever oversight tier was chosen against fatigue and deception.

cases.prompt: Build the per-tool permission matrix and decide which tool calls are irreversible enough to need an approval trigger.
cases.reason: Per-tool blast radius and approval triggers are the LLM03/ASI02 tool boundary; the trust reviewer tests the human side of the gates those triggers fire.
